html:
The Phoenician alphabet is a script of 22 letters, all consonants, used by the Phoenician cities of the Levant from about 1050 BCE. It is the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic alphabets, and so of most alphabets used today.

It grew out of older experiments. Workers in Sinai and Canaan had earlier borrowed a few Egyptian hieroglyphs and used each one for the first sound of a word in their own language. The Phoenicians settled this into a fixed set of signs, written from right to left. One of the oldest long texts in it is carved on the coffin of King Ahiram of Byblos.

Its great advantage was simplicity. Cuneiform and hieroglyphs needed hundreds of signs and years of training. Twenty-two letters could be learned in weeks, so writing was no longer only for professional scribes. Traders could keep their own accounts.

Phoenician traders carried it across the Mediterranean, and it spread in many directions:

  • The Greeks borrowed it around 800 BCE and added letters for vowels, creating the Greek alphabet. From Greek came the Latin alphabet and later Cyrillic.
  • The Aramaic alphabet came from it, and became the script of the Persian Empire. Aramaic in turn gave rise to the square Hebrew alphabet and the Arabic alphabet.
  • In Carthage and the western colonies it lived on as the Punic script into Roman times.

Many letter names and their order still echo it: Phoenician aleph, beth became Greek alpha, beta, and gave us the word "alphabet".
sum: The Phoenician alphabet is a script of 22 letters, all consonants, used by the Phoenician cities of the Levant from about 1050 BCE. It is the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic alphabets, and so of most alphabets used today.
